documentNotes.title: General note.
documentNotes.statement:
Maybe not all problems have correct questions. Some questions (maybe the main question of the problem, maybe one of the subquestions) may have no real sense. In this case you have to write in your answer (in English or Russian): **“impossible situation – ситуация невозможна”**. Of course, this answer has to be explained numerically or logically.

Data from the table of planetary data may be used for solving every problem.

The answers «Да-Yes» or «Нет-No» has to be written in English or Russian.

problems.title: Sirius.
problems.statement: It is known that the so called “Dog Star” (Sirius) is the brightest star in the Chinese sky. And in what else districts on the Earth Sirius is also the brightest star in the real sky of this district? What are numerical characteristics of the borders of these districts? Note: you should take into account only stars in their historical-classical meaning, i.e. Sun, planets, etc. should not be taken into account.

solution.statement:
Sirius is the brightest star (in historical-classical meaning of a star) on the Earth's sky. Therefore in a first approximation it will be the brightest star in those districts on the Earth where it is visible, that is, at least sometimes appears over horizon. As the declination of Sirius is $\delta=-16^\circ43'$, it will be visible in all southern hemisphere, and also in northern hemisphere at latitudes not nearer $16^\circ43'$ to the pole, that is, at latitudes not higher $73^\circ17'$ North. Theoretically, in the second approximation refraction may be taken into account ($35'$ at horizon). With the refraction Sirius can be above horizon at districts till latitudes of $73^\circ52'$ North. But refraction doesn't matter for our goal. There is a talk about **real** (not theoretical) sky in the text.

In the third approximation light absorption should be taken into account. It is obvious that Vega or Arcturus in high sky essentially are more bright than Sirius at horizon. Heights on which Sirius becomes weaker than Vega or Arcturus may be roughly estimated as $\sim5\div8^\circ$. Thus, Sirius is the brightest star in the sky for districts to the south from the latitudes of $65^\circ\div69^\circ$ North.

*Note for jury: the solution without a correct mention of refraction (that is, without mentions that it not effected here) should be estimated with a deduction of 0.5 points. Values $\sim5\div8^\circ$ are approximate, it is important the understanding of the effect and a correct order of this height.*

problems.title: Number of molecules.
problems.statement: Estimate the number of molecules in the Earth's atmosphere.

solution.statement:
The pressure of an atmosphere is the total weight of all number ($N$) of its molecules, distributed over the whole surface of a planet, that is,

$$P=N\cdot m\cdot g/S,$$

where $m$ is the mean value of mass of molecules in atmosphere. Taking into account that the surface of the Earth is

$$S=4\pi R_E^2$$

and mass of molecule is

$$m=\mu/N_A,$$

where $N_A$ is Avogadro number, we can write

$$N=N_A\cdot P\cdot4\pi R_E^2/\mu\cdot g.$$

Since the Earth atmosphere consists mostly on N$_2$ ($\mu_{N2}=28\ \mathrm{g/mol}$) and O$_2$ ($\mu_{O2}=32\ \mathrm{g/mol}$) in approximate proportion 3:1, the mean value of $\mu$ is 29 g/mol or in SI: $2.9\cdot10^{-2}\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$. Calculations:

$$N=6.022\cdot10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\cdot10^5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}\cdot12.6\cdot(6.37\ \mathrm{m}\cdot10^6)^2/2.9\cdot10^{-2}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\cdot9.81\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}=1.08\cdot10^{44}\approx1.1\cdot10^{44}.$$

problems.title: Eris.
problems.statement: The largest discovered now in our Solar system Transneptune body is the dwarf planet Eris (Эрида). Now Eris is near its aphelion point. Find the apparent stellar magnitude of Eris as visible from Earth. Approximately when will the next “Great opposition” of Eris be? What will the magnitude of Eris be as visible from Earth at this “Great opposition”?

solution.statement:
Let us at first answer for the question about the “Great opposition”. And what does it mean the wo… “Great”? The Great oppositions appear for the situation when the distance to opposition planet is small… than during usual (mean) oppositions. In our case it is an opposition when the outer planet is near perihelion. Now Eris is near its aphelion point. From the value of the semiaxis of the Eris' orbit it … evident that its period is of order of centuries and we may talk about the period of the Great oppositions … “years” (in comparison with “weeks” for the Great opposition of Mars) near after of half revolution of th… dwarf planet around the Sun.

The period of Eris can be taken from the table (days should be recalculated into years)

$$T_{Ed}=204852\ \text{days}/365.25\ \text{days/year}=560.85\ \text{years}\approx560\ \text{years}$$

or found from the III Kepler law

$$(T_{Ed}/T_E)^2=(A_{Ed}/A_E)^3,$$

(here and below $A$ means the major semiaxis, $T$ is period, $e$ is eccentricity, $\alpha$ is albedo, $D$ are diameters … the bodies, $R$ are distances, and indexes E, Ed, Sa and S correspond to Earth, Eris, Saturn and Sun).

$$T_{Ed}=T_E\cdot(A_{Ed}/A_E)^{3/2}=1\cdot(68.01)^{3/2}\ \text{years}\approx560\ \text{years}.$$

So the years of the “Great oppositions of Eris” will be after $T_{Ed}/2\approx280$ years.

For the questions of the stellar magnitude there may be a few ways to solve this problem. The main two … them is to compare Eris with some other planet (data can be given from the table) or to calculate it direct… using formulae of the total solar irradiation.

Let us use the first one and compare Eris and, for example, Saturn.

The following aspects should be taken into account:

1. $R_{S\to}$. Distance from the Sun. The intensity of light coming to the bodies is reverse proportional to th… square of these distances.
2. $D$. Size (diameter) of the body. The intensity of light reflecting by the body is proportional to the square of these sizes.
3. $\alpha$. Albedo. The intensity of light reflecting by the body is proportional to the albedos.
4. $R_{E\to}$. Distance from the observer (i.e. from the Earth). The intensity of light coming to the telesco… is reverse proportional to the square of these distances.

The flux to Earth from Eris

$$F_{Ed}\sim\alpha_{Ed}\cdot D_{Ed}^2\cdot(1/R_{E-Ed})^2\cdot(1/R_{S-Ed})^2.$$

The flux to Earth from Saturn

$$F_{Sa}\sim\alpha_{Sa}\cdot D_{Sa}^2\cdot(1/R_{E-Sa})^2\cdot(1/R_{S-Sa})^2.$$

The ratio of fluxes

$$F_{Ed}/F_{Sa}=(\alpha_{Ed}/\alpha_{Sa})\cdot(D_{Ed}^2/D_{Sa}^2)\cdot(R_{E-Sa}\cdot R_{S-Sa})^2/(R_{E-Ed}\cdot R_{S-Ed})^2.$$

For the current situation the following distances should be used:

Since Eris is near its aphelion, $R_{S-Ed}=(1+e)A_{Ed}$, and $R_{E-Ed}=(1+e_{Ed})A_{Ed}\pm A_E$, but, since we do n… know the real configuration of Earth, Sun and Eris (including we do not know the inclination of the Eri… orbit), we should use the average value of $R_{E-Ed}=(1+e_{Ed})A_{Ed}$ as well.

The stellar magnitude for Saturn is given for the mean opposition, so we should not use eccentricity he… $R_{S-Sa}=A_{Sa}$ and $R_{E-Sa}=A_{Sa}-A_E$.

$$F_{Ed}/F_{Sa}=(0.86/0.68)\cdot(2600/120536)^2\cdot(8.584\cdot9.584)^2/(1.434\cdot68.01)^4.$$

$$F_{Ed}/F_{Sa}\approx4.4\cdot10^{-8}.$$

So the difference in magnitudes between the current visible Eris and Saturn in mean opposition is

$$\Delta m=-2^{\mathrm m}.5\cdot\lg(F_{Ed}/F_{Sa})\approx18^{\mathrm m}.4.$$

and the magnitude of Eris

$$m_{Ed}=m_{Sa}+\Delta m=0^{\mathrm m}.7+18^{\mathrm m}.4\approx19^{\mathrm m}.1.$$

The real values that can be found in reports of Eris observations are $18^{\mathrm m}.7\div18^{\mathrm m}.8$.

For the situation of the “Great opposition” of the Eris it is near its perihelion. $R_{S-Ed}=(1-e)A_E$… $R_{E-Ed}\approx(1-e_{Ed})A_{Ed}-A_E$ (here we write “$\approx$” since we do not know the inclination of the Eris' orbit) and n… changed values for Saturn to compare.

$$F_{Ed}/F_{Sa}=(0.86/0.68)\cdot(2600/120536)^2\cdot(8.584\cdot9.584)^2/((0.566\cdot68.01\cdot(0.566\cdot68.01-1))^2).$$

$$F_{Ed}/F_{Sa}\approx1.91\cdot10^{-6}.$$

$$\Delta m=-2^{\mathrm m}.5\cdot\lg(F_{Ed}/F_{Sa})\approx14^{\mathrm m}.3.$$

and the magnitude of Eris in the “Great opposition” is

$$m_{Ed}=m_{Sa}+\Delta m=0^{\mathrm m}.7+14^{\mathrm m}.3\approx15^{\mathrm m}.0.$$

And we should repeat that this way with comparing the Eris and Saturn it is not the only possible correct way for solution.

problems.title: Catastrophe.
problems.statement: Imagine, that on July 5, 2084 the mass of the Sun suddenly has decreased to half its original value. Calculate a new period of revolution of the Earth around of the new Sun.

solution.statement:
At first we should realise that “suddenly decreasing of solar mass to half its original value” is a hypothetic process and many physical laws of conservation cannot be used to compare parameters before and after since the system is not closed. Since no any other changing done, we should assume that at the moment of the mass decreasing other parameters of the Sun and the Earth have not changed: Positions of the Sun and the Earth, velocity of the Earth. Taking into account this postulate, a first approximation, if mass of a central body is reduced to half its original value, the circular speed becomes parabolic one. That is the Earth will move on a parabolic orbit and will never return. The answer to the problem is meaningless (the period is equal to infinity).

Nevertheless, it is known, that on July 5 the Earth is near the aphelion of its orbit. Its speed in this case is less than circular. Thus, in this case if mass of a central body to reduce twice, the speed of the Earth already is less than parabolic, the Earth will be rotate around the Sun on a prolate elliptic orbit.

For the beginning let us find a relation between the speed of the Earth in aphelions $V_{\mathrm{aph}}$ and circular speed $V_0$ for a motion on a circular orbit with the same semi-axis.

Using the II Kepler law one may write

$$V_{\mathrm{per}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{per}}=V_{\mathrm{aph}}\cdot R_{\mathrm{aph}},$$

using the law of conservation of energy

$$V_{\mathrm{per}}^2/2-GM/R_{\mathrm{per}}=V_{\mathrm{aph}}^2/2-GM/R_{\mathrm{aph}},$$

and also taking into account, that

$$R_{\mathrm{per}}=a_0(1-e),\quad R_{\mathrm{aph}}=a_0(1+e),\quad GM=V_0^2\cdot R_0,$$

it is possible to find

$$V_{\mathrm{per}}=V_0\cdot\{(1+e)/(1-e)\}^{1/2},$$

$$V_{\mathrm{aph}}=V_0\cdot\{(1-e)/(1+e)\}^{1/2}.$$

The orbit parameters of the Earth after that the mass of Sun has decreased to half its present value are designate as:

$a_N$ – semi-axis of an orbit,

$T_N$ – period of revolution,

$e_N$ – eccentricity,

$V_N$ – speed for a motion on a circular orbit with a semi-axis $a_N$.

Let us write three additional equations:

distance $R_{\mathrm{aph}}$, former distance in aphilion, became now the distance in perihelion

$$a_0(1+e)=R_{\mathrm{aph}}=R_{\mathrm{per}-N}=a_N(1-e_N),$$

speed $V_{\mathrm{aph}}$, former speed in aphilion, will now become the speed in perihelion

$$V_{\mathrm{aph}}=V_{\mathrm{per}-N}=V_N\cdot\{(1+e_N)/(1-e_N)\}^{1/2},$$

and the relation

$$V_N=2\pi a_N/T_N.$$

By solving all equations together it is possible to receive a beautiful expression

$$a_N=a_0(1+e)/2e.$$

According to the general III Kepler law

$$T_N=T_0\cdot2^{1/2}\cdot(a_N/a_0)^{3/2},$$

one can find

$$T_N=T_0\cdot2^{1/2}\cdot\{(1+e)/2e\}^{3/2}.$$

$$T_N=2^{1/2}\cdot(1.017/0.034)^{3/2}\approx230\ \mathrm{years}.$$

problems.title: Galaxy pair.
problems.statement:
This famous galaxy pair contains two interacting galaxies, IC563 and IC564. The coordinates of the centers of IC563 and IC564 are respectively RA 146.58479, DEC 3.04558 and RA 146.58783, DEC 3.07137. Using the 2.16m telescope of The National Astronomical Observatories of China (NAOC), their R-band image in 2009 has been obtained, which is presented at the fig.1. The spectrum of the center of IC563 is shown at the fig.2.

![](p5-galaxies)

![](p5-spectrum)

sections.statement: In April and September, the right ascension of the sun is about 0.5–2.5 h and 10.5–12.5 h respectively. An… the right ascension of the galaxy is $\mathrm{RA}\approx147^\circ\sim10\mathrm h$. Thus, April is the better choice because i… September the visual position of the galaxies is too close to the sun. Answer: **Apr**.
According to the DECs of the two galaxies, it's easy to find that the upper one is IC564.

The wavelength of H$\alpha$ emission line measured in figure 2 is approximately 6680–6700 Å.

Taking into account (see table of constants) that the laboratory wavelength of H$\alpha$ emission is 6563 Å, th… redshift of the galaxy is approximately:

$$z=(\lambda-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0=(6700-6563)/6563\approx0.02.$$

Since $z\ll1$, the recession velocity of the galaxy is:

$$v=c\cdot z=6000\ \mathrm{km/s}$$

We should choose the filter whose peak value of redshift is close to 6000 km/s. The suitable one is № C4.

According to Hubble's law, the distance to the galaxies is:

$$r=v/H_0=6000\ \mathrm{km/s}/70\ (\mathrm{km/s})/\mathrm{Mpc}\approx85\ \mathrm{Mpc},\ \text{i.e. }85\,000\,000\ \text{parsec}.$$

The two galaxies are close to each other and the curvature of the celestial sphere can be neglected. Th… angular distance of the centers of the galaxies is:

$$\alpha=(\Delta\mathrm{RA}^2+\Delta\mathrm{DEC}^2)^{0.5}$$

Where, $\Delta\mathrm{RA}=(\mathrm{RA1}-\mathrm{RA2})\times\cos(\mathrm{DEC})=0.00303^\circ$, $\Delta\mathrm{DEC}=(\mathrm{DEC1}-\mathrm{DEC2})=0.02579^\circ$. As a result:

$$\alpha=0.02597^\circ=93.5''.$$

The distance between the two galaxies is:

$$d=r\cdot\alpha=85\,000\,000\cdot93.5/3600/57.3=38.5\ \mathrm{kpc}.$$
